book.t: In the Hebrew text, 1:10-11 is 2:1-2, and 2:1-23 is 2:3-25.

1:1.t: Hosea prophesied in the northern kingdom of Israel from about 750 BC until shortly before its fall in 722 BC.

1:4.t: Jezreel means "God sows" or "God scatters". Jehu seized the throne by a massacre at Jezreel (2 Kings 9-10).

1:6.t: Lo-ruhamah means "not loved" or "not shown compassion".

2:1.t: "My people ... My loved one": the KJV's "Ammi ... Ru-hamah", the children's names with "not" removed.

2:15.t: The Valley of Achor ("trouble") was where Achan was stoned (Joshua 7:24-26).

3:1.t: "Sacred raisin cakes": the KJV's "flagons of wine"; cakes used in pagan worship.
"Love her as the LORD loves the Israelites": Hosea's costly love for his unfaithful wife pictures God's love for unfaithful Israel. The Hebrew ahavah is used four times in the verse.

3:2.t: "Fifteen pieces of silver": the Hebrew does not name the unit. "About 330 liters of barley": the KJV's "an homer of barley, and an half homer of barley".

3:4.t: "Sacred stones ... household gods": the KJV's "an image ... teraphim".

4:4.t: The Hebrew of this verse is difficult.

4:7.t: "I will exchange their glory for disgrace": following the KJV and the standard Hebrew. An ancient scribal tradition reads "they exchanged My glory for disgrace".

4:12.t: "A wooden idol ... a diviner's rod": the KJV's "their stocks ... their staff".

4:15.t: Beth Aven ("house of wickedness") is Hosea's mocking name for Bethel ("house of God"), a center of calf worship (1 Kings 12:28-29).

4:18.t: The Hebrew of this verse is difficult.

5:7.t: "He will devour their fields": the KJV's "now shall a month devour them with their portions".

5:13.t: "The great king": the KJV's "king Jareb"; the Hebrew melekh yarev may be a title, "the warrior king".

6:3.t: "Winter rains ... spring rains": the KJV's "the latter and former rain".

6:7.t: "As at Adam": the KJV's "But they like men"; the Hebrew ke'adam can mean "like Adam", "like men" or "at Adam", a town by the Jordan (Joshua 3:16). The word "there" suggests a place.

7:4.t: The images of the oven describe the plots and murders that brought down one king after another in Israel's last years (2 Kings 15).

7:8.t: "A flat loaf not turned over": burnt on one side and raw on the other.

7:14.t: "They gather together": following the KJV and the standard Hebrew. Many Hebrew manuscripts and the Greek read "they slash themselves", a pagan rite (1 Kings 18:28).

8:1.t: "An eagle": the Hebrew nesher can also mean "vulture", a picture of the coming Assyrian army.

8:5.t: The golden calves of Samaria and Bethel were set up by Jeroboam I (1 Kings 12:28-30).

8:10.t: "The mighty king": the KJV's "the king of princes", the king of Assyria.

9:6.t: "Memphis": the KJV's "Memphis", famous for its tombs.

9:9.t: "The days of Gibeah": the outrage of Judges 19-21.

10:9.t: "The days of Gibeah": the outrage of Judges 19-21.

9:10.t: Baal Peor: the Canaanite god Baal as worshiped at Mount Peor, where Israel joined in his worship with the women of Moab; see Numbers 25.

10:1.t: "A spreading vine": the KJV's "an empty vine"; the Hebrew boqeq may mean "luxuriant" or "laid waste".

10:6.t: "The great king": the KJV's "king Jareb"; the Hebrew melekh yarev may be a title, "the warrior king"; see 5:13.

10:12.t: "Reap the fruit of steadfast love": the KJV's "reap in mercy". Some read "until He comes and teaches you righteousness".
"Break up your unplowed ground": prepare your heart to receive God's word. See Jeremiah 4:3.

10:14.t: Shalman may be Shalmaneser V of Assyria or Salamanu, a Moabite king. Beth Arbel is unknown.

11:2.t: "The more they were called": the KJV's "As they called them", following the Hebrew. The Greek reads "As I called them".

11:4.t: "Like one who lifts a little child to the cheek": the KJV's "as they that take off the yoke on their jaws"; the Hebrew ol can mean "yoke" or "infant".

11:8.t: Admah and Zeboyim were destroyed with Sodom and Gomorrah (Deuteronomy 29:23).

"How can I give you up, Ephraim? ... For I am God, and not a man": one of the most tender passages in the prophets. God's anger is real, but His compassion (Hebrew nichumim) overcomes it. His holiness shows itself in mercy, not only in judgment.

11:12.t: In the Hebrew text this verse is 12:1, and 12:1-14 is 12:2-15.

12:4.t: "Talked with him": the KJV's "spake with us", following the Hebrew; the Greek and Syriac read "with him".

12:12.t: "Aram": the KJV's "Syria", the land where Jacob served Laban for his wives. See Genesis 29.

13:2.t: "They offer human sacrifices": the KJV's "Let the men that sacrifice kiss the calves". The Hebrew can be read either way.

13:13.t: The child who will not be born pictures Israel refusing the moment of repentance.

13:14.t: "The grave": Hebrew Sheol. "I will have no compassion": the KJV's "repentance shall be hid from mine eyes".

"Death, I will be your plagues! Grave, I will be your destruction!": Paul quotes this verse from the Greek in his great chapter on the resurrection: "Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting?" (1 Corinthians 15:55).

13:16.t: In the Hebrew text this verse is 14:1, and 14:1-9 is 14:2-10.

14:2.t: "That we may offer the praise of our lips as our sacrifice": the KJV's "so will we render the calves of our lips", following the Hebrew: words of praise offered in place of sacrificial bulls. The Greek reads "the fruit of our lips", quoted in Hebrews 13:15.

1:10.t: and 2:23 "Not My people ... You are My people": Paul and Peter quote these verses of the Gentiles who have become God's people through Christ (Romans 9:25-26, 1 Peter 2:10).

2:16.t: "My husband ... my master" (Hebrew ishi ... ba'ali): the KJV keeps the Hebrew words "Ishi" and "Baali". Ba'al means "master" or "husband", and was also the name of the Canaanite god. Israel will no longer confuse the LORD with Baal.

2:19.t: "I will betroth you to Me forever": God promises a renewed marriage with His people, with five gifts: righteousness (tsedeq), justice (mishpat), steadfast love (hesed), compassion (rachamim) and faithfulness (emunah). The KJV's "lovingkindness, and in mercies". "You will acknowledge the LORD" (veyada'at et YHWH): literally "you will know the LORD", a word used of the intimate knowledge of marriage.

4:1.t: "No faithfulness, no steadfast love, no acknowledgment of God" (Hebrew emet, hesed, da'at elohim): the three things God looks for in His people. "Knowledge" (da'at) is not just information but a relationship of loving loyalty.

4:6.t: "No faithfulness, no steadfast love, no acknowledgment of God" (Hebrew emet, hesed, da'at elohim): the three things God looks for in His people. "Knowledge" (da'at) is not just information but a relationship of loving loyalty.

6:2.t: "On the third day He will restore us": a promise of quick recovery. Christians have heard in it an echo of Christ's resurrection "on the third day" (1 Corinthians 15:4).

6:6.t: "I desire steadfast love, not sacrifice" (Hebrew ki hesed chafatsti velo zavach): the KJV's "I desired mercy, and not sacrifice". Jesus quoted this verse twice (Matthew 9:13, 12:7). The Greek translation used eleos, "mercy".

10:8.t: "They will say to the mountains, 'Cover us!'": Jesus quotes these words on the way to the cross (Luke 23:30); see also Revelation 6:16.

11:1.t: "Out of Egypt I called My son": Matthew 2:15 applies this to the infant Jesus returning from Egypt. Jesus, God's true Son, relives Israel's story and is faithful where Israel failed.

14:4.t: "I will heal their waywardness and love them freely" (Hebrew ohavem nedavah): literally "love them as a freewill offering", spontaneously, without being earned. The book that began with an unfaithful wife ends with God's free and healing love.
